subject: Industrial Engineering
summary: linear programming (graphical method, special cases, simplex and Big-M, duality), transportation (NWC, degeneracy, u–v method), the assignment problem (Hungarian method), project networks (CPM forward and backward pass, floats, PERT time estimates and probability, crashing) and M/M/1 queues

questions.text: Maximise Z = 2x + 3y subject to x + y ≤ 8, x + 3y ≤ 18, 2x + y ≤ 14 and x, y ≥ 0. The maximum value of Z is ______
solution: Concept: The optimum of an LP lies at a corner (extreme point) of the feasible region; evaluate Z at every corner.
Corners: (0, 0); (7, 0) on 2x + y = 14; (6, 2) where 2x + y = 14 meets x + y = 8; (3, 5) where x + y = 8 meets x + 3y = 18; (0, 6)
Maximum Z = 21 at x = 3, y = 5
Exam tip: Check each intersection against the third constraint: x + 3y = 18 and 2x + y = 14 meet at (4.8, 4.4), which violates x + y ≤ 8, so it is not a corner.

questions.text: The LP: maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x − y ≤ 2, x ≥ 1 and x, y ≥ 0 has
solution: Concept: If the feasible region is open in a direction in which Z keeps increasing, the LP is unbounded.
Take x = 1 and let y grow: x − y = 1 − y ≤ 2 holds for every y ≥ 0, so all points (1, y) are feasible
Z = 3 + 2y → ∞: the solution is unbounded (B)
Exam tip: In the simplex table, unboundedness shows up as an entering column with no positive entry (no ratio can be formed).

questions.text: In the Big-M method, a constraint of the type a₁x₁ + a₂x₂ ≥ b (with b > 0) in a maximisation problem is converted to an equation by
opts: subtracting a surplus variable and adding an artificial variable with a coefficient of −M in the objective
adding an artificial variable with a coefficient of +M in the objective
questions.ans: (C) subtracting a surplus variable and adding an artificial variable with a coefficient of −M in the objective
solution: Concept: A surplus variable turns ≥ into =, but it enters with −1, so it cannot form the initial identity basis.
An artificial variable A is added to give a starting basic feasible solution; to drive it out, it is penalised with −M (very large) in a max problem (+M in a min problem): (C)
If an artificial variable stays positive in the final table, the LP is infeasible.
Exam tip: The two-phase method does the same job: phase 1 minimises the sum of artificial variables.

questions.text: Three warehouses S1, S2, S3 with supplies of 30, 50 and 20 units serve four shops D1–D4 with demands of 20, 40, 30 and 10 units. The unit costs (₹) to D1, D2, D3, D4 are: from S1: 3, 1, 7, 4; from S2: 2, 6, 5, 9; from S3: 8, 3, 3, 2. The total cost (in ₹) of the initial basic feasible solution found by the north-west corner rule is ______
solution: Concept: NWC rule: start at the top-left cell, allocate the most possible, and move right (demand left over) or down (supply left over).
Six allocations = m + n − 1 = 3 + 4 − 1, so the solution is non-degenerate.
Exam tip: NWC ignores costs; VAM or the least-cost method usually starts much closer to the optimum.

questions.text: An initial basic feasible solution of an m × n transportation problem has fewer than m + n − 1 positive allocations. Before applying the u–v (MODI) method, one should
opts: drop one row of the cost table
add a dummy row of zero cost
allocate a very small quantity ε to a suitable empty cell that does not form a closed loop with the occupied cells
questions.ans: (D) allocate a very small quantity ε to a suitable empty cell that does not form a closed loop with the occupied cells
solution: Concept: The u–v method needs m + n − 1 occupied (basic) cells to solve for all the ui and vj; fewer cells means the solution is degenerate.
Put ε (→ 0) in an independent empty cell, preferably a low-cost one, so that no closed loop is formed: (D). Then proceed normally and set ε = 0 at the end.
Exam tip: A dummy row or column is used for an unbalanced problem (total supply ≠ total demand), not for degeneracy.

questions.text: Three workers W1, W2, W3 are to be assigned one each to jobs J1, J2, J3. The costs (₹) are W1: 8, 4, 7; W2: 5, 2, 3; W3: 9, 4, 8 (for J1, J2, J3). The minimum total cost (in ₹) is ______
solution: Concept: Hungarian method: subtract row minima, then column minima, and make an assignment using independent zeros.
Row reduction: W1: 4, 0, 3; W2: 3, 0, 1; W3: 5, 0, 4. Column reduction (minima 3, 0, 1): W1: 1, 0, 2; W2: 0, 0, 0; W3: 2, 0, 3
Zeros can be covered by 2 lines (< 3), so subtract the smallest uncovered value 1 and add it at line intersections: W1: 0, 0, 1; W2: 0, 1, 0; W3: 1, 0, 2
Exam tip: With only 3! = 6 possibilities, quickly listing them (15, 16, 16, 17, 18, 18) is a fast check in the exam.

questions.text: To solve an assignment problem in which the entries are profits to be maximised by the Hungarian method, the profit matrix is first
opts: converted to a loss matrix by subtracting every entry from the largest entry of the matrix
multiplied by the number of rows
divided by the largest entry, and then the method is applied unchanged to maximise
questions.ans: (A) converted to a loss matrix by subtracting every entry from the largest entry of the matrix
solution: Concept: The Hungarian method minimises. Maximising P is the same as minimising (Pmax − P) (or −P).
Subtract each entry from the largest one to get an opportunity-loss matrix, then minimise: (A)
The optimal assignment is the same; the total profit is read from the original matrix.
Exam tip: An unbalanced problem (more jobs than workers) needs a dummy row with zero entries first.

questions.text: The activity-on-arrow network of a project is shown, with durations in days. The project duration (in days) is ______
solution: Concept: Forward pass: earliest time of an event Ej = max over incoming activities of (Ei + tij); the project time is E of the end event.
E6 = max(11 + 5, 9 + 9, 2 + 10) = max(16, 18, 12) = 18 days; the critical path is A–E–G (1–2–5–6)
Exam tip: Path lengths: A–C–F 16, B–D–F 15, A–E–G 18, B–H 12. Listing all paths is a quick check in small networks.

questions.text: For the project network of the previous question, the total float of activity D (3–4), in days, is ______
solution: Concept: Total float = LS − ES = Lj − Ei − tij, found from a backward pass.
Free float of D = E4 − E3 − 8 = 11 − 10 = 1 day.
Exam tip: TF of an activity = (critical path length) − (length of the longest path through that activity) = 18 − 15 = 3.

questions.text: An activity has optimistic, most likely and pessimistic times of 3, 6 and 15 days. Its expected time and standard deviation are
solution: Concept: PERT (beta distribution): te = (a + 4m + b)/6, σ = (b − a)/6.
Exam tip: te lies on the side of the longer tail (b − m = 9 > m − a = 3), so it exceeds the most likely time.

questions.text: The expected length of the critical path of a project is 50 days and the variance of the project duration is 25 days². Assuming a normal distribution (z = 1.645 for 95 % probability), the due date (in days) that gives a 95 % chance of completion (round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: T = Te + zσ, where σ is the square root of the sum of the variances of the critical activities.
σ = √25 = 5 days
Exam tip: Never add the standard deviations of activities; add variances and then take the square root.

questions.text: While crashing a project to reduce its duration at minimum extra cost, the activity crashed first is the one
opts: with the longest normal duration in the network
with the least cost slope among all activities
on the critical path with the least cost slope
on a non-critical path with the largest float
questions.ans: (C) on the critical path with the least cost slope
solution: Concept: Only critical activities shorten the project; cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost)/(normal time − crash time).
Choose the critical activity with the least cost slope: (C). When several paths become critical, all of them must be shortened together (choose the cheapest combination).
Stop when the extra direct cost per day exceeds the indirect cost saved per day: that gives the optimum duration.
Exam tip: Crashing a non-critical activity only adds cost, it never shortens the project.

questions.text: Customers arrive at a single-window counter in a Poisson stream at 6 per hour, and the service time is exponential with a mean of 7.5 minutes (M/M/1). The probability that there are at least 3 customers in the system (round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: In an M/M/1 queue Pn = (1 − ρ)ρn, so P(N ≥ k) = ρk.
Exam tip: P(an arriving customer has to wait) = P(N ≥ 1) = ρ = 0.75.

questions.text: In an M/M/1 queue the arrival rate is 3 per hour and the service rate is 4 per hour. The probability that the server is idle and the average number of customers in the queue (excluding the one in service) are
solution: Concept: P0 = 1 − ρ; Lq = ρ²/(1 − ρ) = λ²/[μ(μ − λ)].
Exam tip: L − Lq = ρ always, because the server holds on average ρ customers.

questions.text: A primal LP has 3 constraints (other than non-negativity) and 2 decision variables. Its dual has
solution: Concept: One dual variable for each primal constraint and one dual constraint for each primal variable; the coefficient matrix is transposed.
3 primal constraints → 3 dual variables; 2 primal variables → 2 dual constraints: (A)
The optimal dual variables are the shadow prices of the primal resources.
Exam tip: The dual of the dual is the primal; a primal with many constraints and few variables is often easier to solve through its dual.
